results.content: ByteAsk (YC F26) is an AI C++ engineer backed by a swarm of agents. Give it a C, C++, or CUDA bug, and it returns a tested pull request with proof that the fix works. Trading systems, rockets, cars, and chips run on millions of lines of C and C++, yet AI writes less than 5% of the code accepted into enterprise codebases. ByteAsk reads code the way the build system does, using compile flags and call graphs to understand what actually runs. It also learns the history behind the code from pull requests, Slack conversations, and Jira tickets. Hundreds of ByteAsk agents try different fixes in parallel on the team’s own machines. They build each branch, run tests and sanitizers, use tools like gdb and perf, and return one pull request with the results attached. On Multi-SWE-bench C++, ByteAsk [...] function each call reaches and which change broke it. It also understands what happened years ago. Old tickets, Slack threads, key decisions, discussions on pull requests. Now bite, ask, writes the fix and test it on your own machines, profiling the hot path and measuring again until the latency is back to normal. All this for a fraction of the cost. That was one agent. Right Ask runs hundreds of agents, each on its own machine, investigating, testing alternatives, reviewing each other's, racing to the best fix. Until it all comes down to 1 pull request with the proof attached. AI is already a genes bite. Ask makes it a senior engineer on your code base built by C++ engineers from Optiver and 3rd AI Byte. Ask your AI C++ engineer and a swarm of them. [...] The world's most critical infrastructure runs on C&C, rockets, cars, pacemakers, markets. Decades of code written and kept alive by hand. Now ask a C++ engineer about AI. Because AI guesses, and the C++ compiler won't tell you when it's wrong. In 2012, one bad deployment costs Night Capital $440 million in 45 minutes. The picture an AI agent changing one line in the trading system. It compiles, test pass, then the market opens and latency is 10 times worse. The AI that wrote it can't tell you why, so it lands on the one engineer who knows that code, who's already buried in Slack and Jira. This time he hands it to bite a XANAI C++. results.content:
Codex is a coding agent from OpenAI that runs everywhere you code — in your terminal, code editor, and the cloud. Codex understands complex codebases, plans and implements new features, debugs difficult issues, and provides high-signal code reviews to help your team ship faster and with more confidence.

Cursor helps you fix issues directly from Slack by starting coding agents. These agents can investigate bugs, add new features, update documentation, and more. Cloud agents can solve quick bugs or build ambitious ideas, with the ability to run for hours on the most complex tasks.
